title: Acupressure as a Complementary Method for Body Awareness in the Context of Integrative Palliative and Hospice Care
summary: People with severe, incurable illnesses who require palliative care often suffer from distressing physical and psychosocial symptoms. Acupressure is a touch-based therapy derived from traditional Chinese medicine. Studies have already demonstrated a positive effect on nausea, pain, anxiety, and the quality of life of patients in palliative care. Given the physical changes that occur at the end of life—such as weight loss, lymphedema, and functional limitations—body perception is often altered in patients in palliative care and is perceived as a burden. Improved body awareness can contribute to a more positive self-image and enhance social participation as well as interaction with family members and care staff. Although there is preliminary evidence that acupressure may indirectly improve body awareness, scientific evidence is lacking. The aim of the study is therefore to gather initial evidence regarding the feasibility, acceptance, and potential effects of acupressure on symptom relief and body awareness in various care settings (palliative care unit, palliative care consultation service, specialized outpatient palliative care, hospice).

Patients/Guests:
Pre-intervention (Day 0): Sociodemographic and clinical data, symptom burden (Minimal Documentation System (MIDOS)), body awareness (State Mindfulness Scale – Body Awareness Subscale), brief qualitative interviews on body awareness (Body Image Assessment)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Inpatient or outpatient in the participating institutions (palliative care ward, inpatient palliative consultation service, specialized palliative home care, hospice)
-persistent nausea, pain and/or anxiety
Exclusion criteria:
-Severe cognitive impairment or altered mental status 
-Medical contraindications to acupressure, such as skin lesions, infections, fractures, or other conditions affecting the relevant body areas
